question:
Patient note:
A 54-year-old man arrived to the combined nephrology–pulmonary clinic this afternoon at the request of his primary practitioner to obtain a unified assessment of cardiorespiratory fitness and renal trajectory before he proceeds with enrollment in a home-based hemodialysis education program. He reports that fifteen months ago his serum creatinine rose from a long-standing baseline of 1.4 mg/dL to 2.6 mg/dL, and on last week’s metabolic panel it measured 3.2 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 24 mL/min/1.73 m². Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio at the same draw was 1,120 mg/g. The decline is attributed to eighteen years of type 2 diabetes that began in his late thirties during a commercial driver’s license renewal physical; he has been taking metformin 1 g twice daily supplemented by glipizide 5 mg each morning, checks glucose four times per day with readings usually between 110 and 180 mg/dL, and his most recent glycated hemoglobin from two weeks ago was 7.4 %. Ophthalmology notes from last month document only mild non-proliferative changes without macular edema; he wears corrective lenses but denies visual distortion, pedal ulcers, or episodes of ketoacidosis. In parallel with the renal deterioration he has noticed a gradual reduction in exercise tolerance related both to breathlessness and lower-limb fatigue. He smoked a pack of cigarettes daily from age 18 to 50 (32 pack-years) and quit after a winter hospitalization for pneumonia, yet he still clears one teaspoon of clear sputum each morning and becomes winded after climbing a single flight of stairs. Office spirometry performed three weeks ago demonstrated an FEV1 of 61 % predicted with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.56 and less than 8 % reversibility after inhaled bronchodilator; he now uses tiotropium 18 µg once daily, a fluticasone-salmeterol combination 250/50 µg twice daily, and albuterol two puffs before exertion, replacing the rescue canister every six weeks. He has never required mechanical ventilation, home oxygen, or an intensive-care stay for respiratory failure, but he recalls two outpatient courses of prednisone during exacerbations precipitated by viral illnesses. Five years ago an abdominal ultrasound obtained for vague right upper-quadrant discomfort revealed increased hepatic echogenicity without nodularity, and vibration-controlled transient elastography last winter measured 6.2 kPa. Serial laboratory panels have shown alanine aminotransferase ranging 48–65 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 42–58 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 86 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, serum albumin 4.0 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.1; he has never experienced jaundice, ascites, gastrointestinal bleeding, encephalopathy, or hepatology admission. He denies crushing substernal pain, diaphoresis with exertion, palpitations, syncope, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, or prior angiography, and a treadmill test completed nine months ago for a corporate wellness program achieved 10 metabolic equivalents with no electrocardiographic changes. He likewise reports no episodes of transient speech difficulty, unilateral weakness, vision loss, limb numbness, or carotid procedures, and neurologic screening examinations by his primary clinician have remained intact. There is no history of claudication, rest pain, limb-threatening ischemia, or vascular bypass surgery; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses have been palpable at each visit. He has never undergone chemotherapy, radiation therapy, or surgical resection for malignancy, and age-appropriate cancer screenings—including colonoscopy at 50 and low-dose chest CT last fall—have been unremarkable. He drinks two light beers on Saturday evenings, denies illicit drug use, and has received negative serology for human immunodeficiency virus during hospital admissions for pneumonia and again prior to planned vascular access creation. His father died of complications from hypertension at 78, and his mother is alive at 82 with osteoarthritis; none of his first-degree relatives experienced premature coronary events or cerebrovascular accidents. Medications in addition to those noted include lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, aspirin 81 mg daily, ergocalciferol 50,000 IU monthly, and over-the-counter omega-3 supplements; he has no known drug allergies and avoids non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, hemoptysis, dyspepsia, hematemesis, melena, dysuria, rash, or arthralgia beyond mild lumbar stiffness after long driving shifts. On examination he appears well nourished, converses in full sentences, and is oriented to person, place, and time. Vital signs: temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 136/78 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 76 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 95 % breathing ambient air, and body-mass index 30 kg/m². Jugular venous pulsation measures 4 cm above the sternal angle, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, and S1 and S2 are crisp with no murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Chest inspection reveals an increased anteroposterior diameter; auscultation detects diminished breath sounds with end-expiratory wheezes diffusely but no crackles. The abdomen is soft and non-tender; the liver edge is not palpable, there is no splenomegaly, and shifting dullness is absent. Extremities are warm without edema; radial, femoral, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses are 2 + bilaterally, capillary refill is under two seconds, and no skin ulcers or hair loss are present. Neurologic testing shows intact cranial nerves II–XII, 5/5 strength throughout, symmetric reflexes, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, and steady tandem gait. Laboratory data drawn in clinic confirm sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 5.0 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 46 mg/dL, creatinine as noted 3.2 mg/dL, calcium 8.5 mg/dL, phosphorus 4.8 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, white-cell count 6.4 × 10⁹/L, platelets 258 × 10⁹/L, fasting glucose 158 mg/dL, HbA1c 7.4 %, AST 52 U/L, ALT 61 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, and INR 1.1. Urinalysis shows 2 + protein, trace blood, and no cells or casts. A post-bronchodilator spirometry printout handed in by the patient confirms the earlier values, and a plain posteroanterior chest radiograph obtained today reveals hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms but clear parenchyma and a normal cardiac silhouette. A 12-lead electrocardiogram performed in clinic shows normal sinus rhythm at 74 beats/min, axis within normal limits, no Q waves, and no ST-segment deviation. He seeks counseling on timing of arteriovenous fistula creation, optimization of inhaler technique to reduce dyspnea during home dialysis training sessions, monitoring of hepatic enzymes while his medication burden increases, and strategies to maintain glycemic control once dietary protein intake is liberalized for dialysis preparation.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) adds age points to weighted comorbidity points:
- Age 54 (50–59 years) → 1.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: persistent airflow obstruction with FEV1/FVC 0.56 and maintenance inhaler use → 1.
- Diabetes with end-organ damage: diabetic nephropathy and retinopathy → 2. Do not also count uncomplicated diabetes.
- Moderate-to-severe renal disease: creatinine 3.2 mg/dL exceeds the CCI threshold of 3 mg/dL, with eGFR 24 → 2. Dialysis is not required to meet this criterion.
- Other categories → 0. Hepatic steatosis is suggested, but chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis is not documented under the classic CCI liver criteria.
Total = 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6.
Final answer: 6
